definition: The first actuality of a natural organized body having life potentially; cause of the living body in three senses (efficient, final, formal); the central definiendum of the entire treatise.
notes: Central term of the entire treatise. Predecessors define through movement/cognition/elemental composition; Aristotle's hylomorphic definition replaces all.

definition: The process by which a sense-faculty transitions from potentiality to actuality through the agency of an external object; receives sensible forms without matter.
notes: Second mark attributed to soul by predecessors (DA I); general theory developed in II.5; wax-signet principle in II.12; three-tier reliability in III.3.

definition: Movement resulting from actual exercise of a power of sense; capacity to produce and retain images in the absence of the sensed object. Subdivided into sensitive (all animals) and deliberative (calculative animals only).
notes: "Imagination" imports creative connotations absent from Greek; Schofield, Nussbaum, Caston prefer "appearance" or "representation." Etymology from phaos (light, 429a2-4). First appears in II.8 (voice requires phantasia) before full treatment in III.3.

definition: The product of phantasia; persists in sense-organs after sensation ceases; serves the thinking soul as quasi-perceptual content.
notes: Critical bridge between perception and thought: 'the soul never thinks without a phantasma' (431a17). Objects of thought are 'in the sensible forms' (432a5).

definition: The thinking part of the soul; impassible, unmixed, capable of receiving intelligible forms; divided into active (separable, immortal) and passive (perishable).
notes: Anaxagoras' term adopted in DA I; developed fully in III.4-5. The active/passive labels (nous poiētikos / pathētikos) are post-Aristotelian (Alexander of Aphrodisias).

definition: Technical term for soul's relation to body; soul is first actuality (possession, hexis) distinguished from second actuality (exercise, energeia).
notes: Relationship between entelecheia and energeia debated; some (Sachs) insist on distinction ('being-at-work-staying-itself' vs. 'being-at-work'), others treat as synonymous. Mentioned in DA I.1 as possible characterization; becomes the defining term in II.1.

definition: Three-grade schema: first potentiality (capacity to learn), second potentiality/first actuality (hexis), second actuality (active exercise). Body is matter = potentiality.
notes: The three-grade potentiality/actuality schema of II.5 is the theoretical backbone of the entire treatise's treatment of perception, phantasia, and nous.

definition: Second actuality = active exercise; light as energeia of the transparent; joint actualization of sense and sensible.
notes: Used for active exercise of knowledge and for the joint actualization of sense and sensible (one event, two in being).

definition: In DA I: the mark predecessors attribute to soul (refuted). In DA III: phantasia IS a kinēsis; animal movement from appetite + thought/imagination.
notes: Major semantic shift between Books I and III: from the property falsely attributed to soul by predecessors to the defining genus of phantasia and the product of the appetitive faculty.

definition: Soul as form of the body; sense receives the eidos of objects without their matter.
notes: Critical in two contexts: (1) soul as eidos/form (II.1), (2) sense receives eidos without hulē (II.12 wax-signet). The topos eidōn (place of forms, 429a27) applies to the thinking soul only potentially.

definition: Body is matter/potentiality to soul's form/actuality; sense receives form without matter; plants affected by forms with matter (hence no perception).
notes: The form/matter polarity is the ontological backbone of the hylomorphic psychology.

definition: Three senses: matter, form, composite. Soul is substance as form.
notes: Presupposes Metaphysics Z-H on substance. The three-sense distinction is the launching point for the soul-definition.

definition: Generic desiderative faculty covering boulēsis (wish), thumos (spirit), epithumia (appetite proper); with practical thought, the source of animal locomotion.
notes: Barnes' 'appetite' narrows the term; 'desire' (Hicks, Hamlyn) better captures generic scope. The single moving faculty in the practical domain.

definition: Faculty that discriminates between objects of different senses in a single indivisible act; numerically one in exercise but divisible in being.
notes: Bridges the individual senses to the unified perceptual field; prerequisite for phantasia's cross-modal image production.

definition: Multiple senses in DA: (1) enmattered accounts (logoi enuloi) of psychic states, (2) sense-organ as a logos/ratio between contraries, (3) sense receives form 'according to its logos', (4) voice as sound with logos (meaning).
notes: Polysemy across the treatise: methodological (logoi enuloi), perceptual (ratio of the mean), semantic (meaningful speech). Connects to the BCAP and Rhetoric pipelines.

definition: Soul as formal cause; the essence is identical with the cause of its being.
notes: Links soul-as-cause to the Metaphysics Z-H essence doctrine.

definition: Soul is cause in three senses: efficient (source of movement), final (for-the-sake-of-which), formal (essence).
notes: Applies Physics II.3 four-cause framework; only three of four causes are attributed to soul (material cause is the body).

definition: Nature acts for an end; all natural bodies are organs of soul. Two senses: end achieved, and being in whose interest.
notes: The teleological dimension of soul-as-cause; connects to the practical architecture of DA III (good as unmoved mover of action).

definition: Movement, rest, figure, magnitude, number, unity -- perceived non-incidentally by more than one sense.
notes: Critical for phantasia: these cross-modal contents are what phantasia inherits and re-presents in the absence of the object. Most liable to perceptual error (428b22-25).

definition: Sense-organ as mean between contraries it perceives; explains discriminative power and vulnerability to excess.
notes: Connects to the NE/BCAP mesotēs doctrine but here applied to perception, not virtue.

definition: Sound proper to ensouled beings; requires imagination (phantasia) and meaning (sēmantikos); produced by windpipe, lungs, and the soul.
notes: Earliest explicit linkage of perception and phantasia in the treatise. Connects to BCAP distinction between logos and phōnē.

definition: The one sense indispensable for animal existence; excess destroys the animal itself. Grounds intelligence claim: man's flesh is the most discriminating.
notes: Problematizes the medium doctrine (flesh as medium, not organ). Touch grounds the embodied-intelligence thesis critical for the dissertation.

definition: The states of the soul (anger, fear, etc.) that are shared with the body; require enmattered definitions (logoi enuloi).
notes: The I.1 analysis of pathē establishes the hylomorphic method. Connects to Rhetoric II pathē and BCAP FP3 treatment.

definition: The view that soul is a ratio or blending of bodily contraries; refuted because harmony admits of degrees while soul does not.
notes: One of the three predecessor views systematically refuted in Book I.
